parts.name: frame
parts.text: Start with the frame, motor plate to the left and the end rib to the right. It printed baseplate-down. 180.6 mL, just under four hours, and it is the one part a wrong guess could have scrapped.

parts.name: 608 bearing
parts.text: Press the 608 into the end rib from the OUTSIDE until it seats on the 2 mm shoulder. The pocket is drawn 22.20 and prints about 21.96 on a 22.00 bearing, so it wants thumb pressure and should not fall out. If it drops in loose, stop: the rest of the screw train is built on this being tight.

parts.name: LM8UU x2
parts.text: Press the two LM8UU bushes into the carriage bores, one each side. Same story as the 608: drawn 8.24, prints about 8.00. Do this before anything goes on the rods, because the carriage cannot be fitted to them afterwards.

parts.name: T8 anti-backlash nut
parts.text: Bolt the anti-backlash nut to the -X face of the carriage, flange into the counterbore, four M3 on a 16 mm circle. Check the nut you actually received first: 22.0 flange, 3.5 thick, 16.0 bolt circle, 10.6 body. A plain brass nut will bolt up and give away 0.1 to 0.3 mm at every reversal, which lands on the foot of systole.

parts.name: carriage
parts.text: The carriage is now a sub-assembly: two bushes and the nut. Hold it between the rails at the motor end, roughly on the screw axis. Nothing holds it there yet.

parts.name: 8 mm shafts x2
parts.text: Slide the two hardened 8 mm shafts in from the motor end, through the carriage bushes, into the seats at the rib end. They must be HARDENED, not 304 stainless: a recirculating ball bush brinells soft shafting and the carriage then rumbles. Teardrop bores, so they print round and the shafts press rather than rattle.

parts.name: Tr8x8 lead screw
parts.text: Feed the lead screw in from the motor end, through the nut, into the 608. Verify the lead BEFORE it goes in: mark the screw, turn it exactly one revolution, and measure the carriage. It must move 8 mm. If it moves 2 mm you have a Tr8x2, which needs four times the rpm and will not do the job at 12 V.

parts.name: 5-8 mm coupler
parts.text: Flexible coupler onto the screw, 8 mm bore to the screw and 5 mm to the motor. Leave the motor-side grub screws loose for now.

parts.name: NEMA 17 pancake
parts.text: Four M3 through the motor plate into the pancake. Slide the shaft into the coupler and tighten both grub screws. The plate is full width and takes any NEMA 17, so the 48 mm motor bolts on in the same holes if the pancake ever runs short of torque.

parts.name: plunger
parts.text: The plunger is the piston. Everything upstream of it exists to move this 12.36 mm column of water 4.17 mm per beat, 70 percent of it inside 100 ms. Leave it long for now; the clamp goes on last.

parts.name: syringe barrel
parts.text: Snap the two split collars onto the barrel first, then lay the whole thing into the saddle with the finger flange hard against the end rib. The flange measures 2.0 and the rib was printed for 2.5, so there is 0.5 mm of slack: the piston's reaction pushes the barrel forward into the rib, and the straps hold it.

parts.name: split collars x2
parts.text: The collars are the only part that knows the barrel is 14.0 mm. They are SPLIT, slit at the top, and the bore is drawn 0.10 mm under the barrel so they snap on and stay put. Slit upward, so pressing the assembly into the saddle closes it rather than spreading it. If you ever change syringe, these two are the only parts you reprint.

parts.name: saddle cap + ties
parts.text: Drop the cap over the collars and run a zip tie through each pair of slots, down through the frame and back. Snug, not crushing: the collar wall is 0.93 mm and it is holding a syringe, not a driveshaft.

parts.name: rod clamp
parts.text: Last. Drop the plunger disc into the carriage pocket, lay the clamp tongue into the rod slot, and run two M3 x 16 down into the carriage. The bar should still stand about 1.25 mm proud when the tongue touches the rod; the bolts close that gap and pin the rod. This is what makes the whole drive independent of the thumb disc, which read 1.9 on a caliper, 2.0 on another syringe, and 1.71 on a micrometer.
